subject: ss-medical-oncology
title: Radiation oncology essentials for the medical oncologist

steps.tx: The biophysical model describing radiation clonogenic survival relies on quadratic equation mathematics. The **linear-quadratic model** quantifies radiation **cell kill**, where the linear alpha parameter reflects lethal double-strand DNA breaks from single electron tracks, and the quadratic beta parameter represents accumulated sub-lethal breaks from independent tracks. This fundamental relationship governs modern fractionation schedules and equivalent dose calculations in clinical radiation oncology.
steps.say: The biophysical model describing radiation clonogenic survival relies on quadratic equation mathematics. The linear-quadratic model quantifies radiation cell kill, where the linear alpha parameter reflects lethal double-strand DNA breaks from single electron tracks, and the quadratic beta parameter represents sub-lethal breaks from independent tracks. This relationship governs modern fractionation schedules.

steps.tx: Differential tissue responses to altered fraction sizes depend upon the target tissue repair capacity. The **alpha to beta ratio** describes tissue **fractionation sensitivity**, with acutely responding tissues and most carcinomas having a high ratio around 10 Gy, while late-responding tissues like spinal cord and kidneys have a low ratio of 2 to 3 Gy. Large fraction sizes selectively spare early-responding tissues while disproportionately increasing late-tissue necrosis.

left.title: High Alpha/Beta (~10 Gy)
points: Most epithelial carcinomas and high-grade lymphomas
Linear curve dominates at conventional low doses
Fractionation size has relatively minimal impact

right.title: Low Alpha/Beta (2 to 3 Gy)
points: Late-responding tissues (spinal cord, lung, kidney, brain)
Prominent shoulder on cell survival curve
Highly sensitive to fraction size changes (> 2 Gy)

steps.tx: Classical radiobiology explains the clinical efficacy of fractionated therapeutic radiation through cellular dynamics. The **four Rs of radiobiology** comprise **repair** of sub-lethal DNA damage, repopulation of surviving clonogens, redistribution into sensitive cell cycle phases, and reoxygenation of hypoxic tumour cells. Fractionating treatment into daily 1.8 to 2.0 Gy fractions allows normal tissues to repair sub-lethal damage while selectively sensitizing tumour cells through reoxygenation and cell cycle redistribution.
steps.say: Classical radiobiology explains the clinical efficacy of fractionated therapeutic radiation through cellular dynamics. The four Rs of radiobiology comprise repair of sub-lethal DNA damage, repopulation of surviving clonogens, redistribution into sensitive cell cycle phases, and reoxygenation of hypoxic tumour cells. Fractionation allows normal tissues to repair damage while sensitizing tumours.

rows: Enzymatic repair of sub-lethal DNA breaks
Cells cycle out of resistant S phase into G2-M
Synchronizes tumour cells into radiosensitive phases
Prolonging overall treatment time reduces local control
Hypoxic cells gain access to capillary blood
Alleviates hypoxia, enhancing oxygen-mediated DNA fixation

steps.tx: This figure follows a beam from the **linear accelerator** through cell kill to tissue effects. Shaped photon fields strike the tumour while the gantry rotates, and killing works directly on DNA and indirectly through free radicals, with oxygen sharpening the effect. Small daily **fractions** let normal tissue repair between doses. The four Rs explain the schedule, and acute injury is set against late fibrosis, necrosis and second malignancy.
steps.say: Start at the machine and describe how the beam is shaped and aimed. Then explain the two routes of cell killing and why oxygen matters. State why the dose is split into small daily fractions and what each of the four Rs contributes. End by contrasting early reversible injury with late permanent damage and the small lifelong risk the figure names.

vis.alt: Linear accelerator beam on a tumour, a daily fractionation chart sparing normal tissue, the four Rs of radiobiology and acute and late effects.
vis.caption: Radiotherapy principles: LINAC, fractionation and the four Rs.

steps.tx: Localized ionizing radiation can unexpectedly trigger out-of-field systemic antitumor immunity. The **abscopal effect** describes regression of distant, non-irradiated metastatic tumour lesions following localized radiotherapy, mediated by **systemic immune activation**. Radiation-induced cell death exposes tumour neoantigens and releases damage-associated molecular patterns, stimulating dendritic cells to cross-prime tumor-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes.

steps.tx: Combining systemic cytotoxics with localized radiation produces synergistic locoregional tumor control. **Concurrent chemoradiation** utilizes **radiosensitizing** cytotoxic agents, predominantly **cisplatin** or **fluorouracil**, to inhibit the repair of sub-lethal radiation damage and synchronize tumour cells at the radiosensitive G2-M cell cycle transition. This combined modality approach represents the definitive standard of care for locally advanced head and neck, cervical, and gastrointestinal carcinomas.
steps.say: Combining systemic cytotoxics with localized radiation produces synergistic locoregional tumor control. Concurrent chemoradiation utilizes radiosensitizing cytotoxic agents, predominantly cisplatin or fluorouracil, to inhibit the repair of sub-lethal radiation damage and synchronize tumour cells at the radiosensitive G2-M transition. This represents standard care for cervical and head and neck cancers.

left.title: Radiosensitization Mechanisms
points: Inhibition of sub-lethal radiation DNA repair
Synchronisation at G2-M cell cycle checkpoint
Depletion of endogenous intracellular radioprotective thiols

right.title: Clinical Indications for Concurrent Cisplatin
points: Locally advanced cervical carcinoma (FIGO IB3 to IVA)
Definitive locally advanced squamous head and neck cancer
Unresectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer

steps.tx: Prior radiation exposure permanently alters microvascular bed architecture, predisposing to localized recall toxicities. **Radiation recall** dermatitis presents as acute inflammatory skin **erythema** at a previously irradiated site triggered by subsequent administration of taxanes, anthracyclines, or **gemcitabine**. Manifesting as erythema, desquamation, and vesicular ulceration weeks to months post-radiation, management mandates chemotherapy suspension and topical or systemic corticosteroids.

steps.tx: Direct intracavitary or interstitial radiation placement achieves highly localized conformality. **Brachytherapy** places sealed **radioisotopes** directly within or immediately adjacent to tumour tissue, delivering exceptionally high radiation doses to target neoplastic cells while exploiting the inverse-square law of radiation physics to achieve rapid dose fall-off, sparing adjacent critical normal organs in cervical, prostate, and breast carcinomas.

rows: High-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy in cervix and breast
Permanent interstitial seed implant for prostate carcinoma
Episcleral eye plaques for uveal melanoma

steps.tx: Patients with limited metastatic dissemination represent a unique clinical entity amenable to local ablation. **Oligometastatic cancer** defined as 1 to 5 discrete metastases benefits from aggressive local therapy, where **consolidative radiotherapy** using stereotactic body radiotherapy SBRT significantly improves progression-free and overall survival in randomized phase 2 trials such as SABR-COMET. Delivering ablative biological doses over 1 to 5 fractions achieves long-term disease control in oligometastatic prostate, breast, and lung carcinomas.
